About Asia Centre

Founded in 2005, Asia Centre is an independent research institute that holds debates and issues publications on matters relating to international, strategic, economic relations, as well as the political and social transformations underway in the Asia-Pacific region. At the crossroads of university research as well as public and private decision-making, Asia Centre researchers identify critical regional issues and analyse them in-depth, taking into consideration both local and global dimensions. Asia Centre’s programs are developed with a vast network of partners, companies and major specialist centres in Europe, North America and Asia. The Centre carries out joint operations with these groups, for a better. interpretation of ideas and issues. The conclusions of these meetings, such as the results of the work carried out using original sources by our researchers, are widely distributed through the Centre’s publications as well as through international journals, books and medias.

About the Prix Asia Centre

Asia Centre launched an exciting new initiative to foster fresh perspectives and innovative research on China’s foreign policy and its global interactions: the Prix Asia Centre, first edition. The theme of the 2025 edition was “China’s Geopolitics”.

About the author, Thomas Mikan

Graduated from Sciences Po Strasbourg with a master’s degree in Negotiations and International Expertise, Thomas MIKAN has carried out several academic projects on various historical and contemporary topics related to Asia, especially China, Japan and Southeast Asia. Particularly interested in the relations between Asian countries and Africa, he further broadened and refined his knowledge of the Asian region through an exchange year at Keio University in Tokyo. Finally, he completed a long-term internship in a foundation devoted to economic diplomacy between France and Asia.

##### Abstract

Based on scientific literature and Asian issues press, this paper examines the multifaceted relations between China and its immediate neighbour, Mongolia. It first provides an overview of the evolving dynamics of Sino-Mongolian relations from the mid-20th century to the early 2010s, marked by the Sino-Soviet dispute and Mao Zedong’s irredentist ambitions and the renewal of the bilateral relations after the collapse of the USSR. It then analyses the contemporary challenges shaping the Sino-Mongolian relationship, with particular attention to economic cooperation through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), which reveals a significant asymmetry in the context of the recent crisis – the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine – which have reconfigured these relations. Lastly, it highlights the inherent fragility of these ties, focusing on tensions surrounding the Dalai Lama and China's concerns about Mongolia’s Third Neighbour Policy. This essay ultimately demonstrates how Mongolia has become a strategic component of China’s regional ambitions in Northeast Asia while also emphasizing that the relations remain complex, asymmetrical and influenced by broader geopolitical shifts.

Chinese Mongolian Diplomatic Relations

Thomas Mikan

Prix Asia Centre 2025

China and Mongolia have shared close, complex and tumultuous relations since at least the 12th century when Genghis Khan unified Mongol tribes and laid the foundations of the Mongol empire, automatically affecting Northern Chinese societies. At its apogee, the Mongol Empire, after decades of warfare, conquered the entire territory of China and established the Yuan dynasty until its collapse in 1368, replaced by the Ming dynasty, an ethnic Han Chinese regime while Mongolia was disintegrating into multiple factions. In the 17th century, the Qing Empire overcame the Ming dynasty and took control over Mongolia and incorporated it into its inner territory until the beginning of the 20th century. Indeed, the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911 allowed Mongolia to gain more autonomy although the newly proclaimed Chinese Republic kept claiming its sovereignty over Mongolia’s lands.

The aftermath of the Russian Revolution and the birth of the Soviet Union drastically impacted Chinese Mongolian relations. Indeed, the USSR acted as a symbolic support to Mongolia against China by fostering a Socialist revolution in Mongolia which culminated in the establishment of the Mongolian People’s Republic (MPR) in 1924, a satellite state of Moscow in Northeast Asia. This Soviet Mongolian rapprochement widened the gap between Beijing and Ulaanbaatar until the post-World War II period and the proclamation of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in 1949.

1°) Sino-Mongolian relations from the mid-20th century to the early 2010s

Chinese Communist views on Mongolia and the Sino-Soviet split

Even though the Chinese Nationalist government had recognised the independence of Mongolia, Chinese communists expressed their reluctance to consider MPR as an autonomous state claiming their sovereignty over Outer Mongolia whereas Beijing recognized Mongolian in 1949 and both opened an embassy in each other’s states in 1950. In this context, the recognition of Mongolia was an essential part of the forthcoming Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance between Beijing and Moscow (Her, E. (1997), The Great Game : Mongolia between Russia and China, The Mongolian Journal of International Affairs, 4, p.66). Despite this agreement, Mao Zedong’s irredentist desires over Mongolia persisted. Indeed, during Nikita Khrushchev’s diplomatic journey to China in 1954, Mao, through his Prime Minister Zhou Enlai, informed the Soviet leader that the Chinese aspiration to acquire the whole Mongolian territory did not belong to the past. However, the Soviets officially refused to modify the status of MPR. Thus, to soften the influence of the USSR in Mongolia, Beijing exacerbated the pan-Mongolian sentiment by building a mausoleum to the glory of Genghis Khan in Inner Mongolia whereas he was born in Outer Mongolia (Her, 1997). Likewise, in 1956, Mao Zedong attempted to intervene within Mongolia’s domestic affairs by sending over 300 000 Han Chinese workers to rebuild its economy (Kasim, M. (2024), Mongolia’s development and

5/11

increasing dependence on China, Saka Journals, p.119). Nevertheless, Mongolian government declined Chinese aid, considering that 300 000 non-Mongolian ethnic group people were a disproportionate number relative to the country’s population (800 000 at this time). Obviously, this offer was a part of a broader strategy which aimed to bring Mongolia back into Beijing’s sphere of influence (Kasim, 2024). Along the same lines, China tried to normalize its relations with Mongolia as shown by the two Zhou Enlai’s trips to Mongolia (1952, 1954) and the three Tsedenbal Yumjaa’s journeys to China (1952, 1959 and 1962). In 1960, Beijing and Ulaanbaatar signed a Friendship and Mutual Assistance Agreement on economy, science and technology issues, reinforcing this trend.

The 1950s coincided with the erosion of Sino-Soviet relations and Mongolia became a fully fledged issue in this confrontation. Indeed, sharing a border with both China and the Soviet Union, Ulaanbaatar tried to advocate for neutrality, but the regional circumstances obliged it to take sides against one of them. That is the reason why Mongolia decided to support the USSR and joined the COMECON in 1962 (Her, 1997). While the USSR tried to contain Mongolian nationalism, China kept encouraging it. Still in 1962, the MPR government organized a commemoration in honour of Genghis Khan’s 800th anniversary, symbolically supported by the PRC meanwhile prompting the anger of Soviet Union authorities (Her, 1997).

1964 marked a turning point in Chinese Mongolian relations. On July 2, 1964, Beijing and Ulaanbaatar ratified a boundary treaty (signed in early 1963) which officially and permanently delimits the border (4700 km long) between them. This treaty had two main objectives for China. To begin with, it reassured Mongolia and put an end to Mao’s irredentist views towards Outer Mongolia. Furthermore, China also hoped that this rapprochement would counterbalance Soviet Mongolian relations and restore balance to the trilateral relations between Mongolia, USSR and China in favour of Beijing (Her, 1997).

After two decades of Sino-Soviet dispute, the late 20th century prefigured a new phase of the Chinese Mongolian relations. The repression of 1989 Tiananmen Square protests paved the way for Mongolia's 1990 Democratic Revolution in Mongolia (Maire, A. (2021), La Mongolie d'aujourd'hui, Asia Focus, 158, p.4). Indeed, Mongolian Communist authorities were completely aware of the urgent need to reform their country. Unlike China, Ulaanbaatar did not resort to violence as a means of repression and decided to guide Mongolian society towards a democracy and market economy peacefully. Finally, during this period, China served as a counter-model to Mongolia (Maire, 2021).

The collapse of the Soviet Union and the renewal of the Chinese Mongolian relations

The fall of the USSR in 1991 reshuffled the deck between China and Mongolia. Throughout the communist era, Ulaanbaatar had chosen the Soviet Union as a model of society and development, but its breakup enabled Mongolia to pivot toward Beijing instead of Moscow. This marked the beginning of the “honeymoon period” (Bondaz, A. (2014) Mongolia: China’s perfect neighbour?, China Analysis, 2014, p.8) between China and Mongolia, characterized by a simultaneous diplomatic, economic and cultural rapprochement. Indeed, in 1994, China and Mongolia signed the Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation based on the principle of “good

6/11

neighbourly relations and cooperation”, defining the core foundations of the future Sino Mongolian bilateral relations. In fact, these relations were strengthened by successive state visits on both sides. Between 1998 and 2003, Chinese Presidents Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao visited Mongolia twice while the President of Mongolia, Bagabandi Natsag went to China once (Lkhaajav, B. (2024 October 15), Mongolia and China celebrate 75 years of partnership, The Diplomat). This partnership was reiterated during Hu Jintao’s visit to Mongolia in 2003. This trip also aimed to concretize the impending joining of Mongolia to the recently shaped and Chinese-led Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) as an observer country (Lkhaajav, 2024).

From the late 1990s to the early 2010s, the diplomatic proximity between China and Mongolia significantly boosted economic exchanges. In 1999, China overtook Russia and became Mongolia's primary economic partner regarding economic issues thanks to a strategy based on soft and concessional loan agreements (Lkhaajav, 2024). The exchanges occurred as follows: Mongolia exported raw materials (coal, timber) to China while Beijing provided technology and financial investments to Ulaanbaatar.
